topics.title: Average speed, rate of change of speed and the ramp practical

cards.front: Equation for average speed from distance and time
cards.back:
In words: average speed = distance moved divided by time taken.

In symbols: $v = \frac{d}{t}$

Units: speed m/s, distance m, time s.

Rearranged: $d = v \times t$ and $t = \frac{d}{v}$.

No physics equation is printed in the paper, so this must be recalled.

cards.front: Equation for average speed from an initial and a final speed
cards.back:
In words: average speed = (initial speed + final speed) divided by 2, in m/s.

Use it when the speed changes at a steady rate.

Rearranged: final speed = (2 x average speed) - initial speed.

cards.front: Equation for rate of change of speed
cards.back:
In words: rate of change of speed = (final speed - initial speed) divided by time taken.

Units: both speeds in m/s, time in s, answer in m/s².

Rearranged: final speed = initial speed + (rate x time).

cards.front: Rate of change of speed
cards.back:
Metres per second squared, written **m/s²**.

It says how many metres per second the speed changes in each second.

cards.front: Distance moved, speed and time
cards.back:
Distance: metres (m). Speed: metres per second (m/s). Time: seconds (s).

Convert first: km to m by x1000, minutes to s by x60, km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6.

cards.front: A trolley moves 2.4 m down a runway in 0.8 s. Average speed?
cards.back:
**3 m/s**

average speed = distance / time = 2.4 / 0.8 = 3 m/s

cards.front: A car speeds up from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 s. Rate of change of speed?
A ball-bearing starts from rest and reaches 12 m/s at the foot of a ramp. Average speed over the run?
cards.back:
**6 m/s**

average speed = (0 + 12) / 2 = 6 m/s

cards.front: Prescribed Practical P1: how the average speed down a runway depends on the slope
cards.back:
1 Raise one end of the runway and measure that height with a metre rule.
2 Release the trolley or ball-bearing from the same mark each time.
3 Time it over a measured distance with a stopclock; repeat and take a mean.
4 average speed = distance / time.
5 Repeat for several heights and plot average speed against height.

cards.front: Trap: your number is right but you started from the wrong equation. What do you score?
cards.back:
**Nothing.** A wrong physics equation scores no marks even when the final number is correct.

Write the correct equation on its own line first, then substitute. That equation line is normally a mark by itself.
cards.source: CER March 2026 P1; Physics subject-specific instructions

topics.title: Vectors and scalars; velocity, acceleration and retardation

cards.front: Define a scalar quantity
cards.back:
A quantity that has **size only**, with no direction.

Distance, speed and rate of change of speed are scalars.

cards.front: Define a vector quantity
cards.back:
A quantity that has **size and direction**.

Displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors.

cards.front: In each pair, which is the vector, and do the two share a unit?
cards.back:
Displacement (vector) with distance (scalar), both in m.
Velocity with speed, both in m/s.
Acceleration with rate of change of speed, both in m/s².

The unit never separates them; only direction does.

cards.front: Equation for average velocity
cards.back:
In words: average velocity = displacement divided by time.

In symbols: $v = \frac{d}{t}$, where $d$ is displacement in m.

Units: m/s, m, s. Rearranged: $d = vt$, $t = \frac{d}{v}$.

cards.front: Equation for average velocity from an initial and a final velocity
cards.back:
In words: average velocity = (initial velocity + final velocity) divided by 2.

In symbols: average velocity $= \frac{u + v}{2}$, in m/s.

Only set for motion in one direction.

cards.front: Equation for acceleration
cards.back:
In words: acceleration = (final velocity - initial velocity) divided by time taken.

In symbols: $a = \frac{v - u}{t}$

Units: a in m/s², u and v in m/s, t in s.

Rearranged: $v = u + at$ and $t = \frac{v - u}{a}$.

cards.front: What is retardation?
cards.back: A **negative acceleration**: the object is slowing down, so the final velocity is smaller than the initial velocity and $a$ works out negative.

cards.front: u = 5 m/s, v = 25 m/s, t = 4 s. Acceleration?

topics.title: Distance-time, speed-time, displacement-time and velocity-time graphs

cards.front: On a distance-time graph, what does the gradient give you?
cards.back:
The **speed**: gradient = change in distance / change in time, in m/s.

A steeper line means a faster object; a horizontal line means it is stationary.

image.alt: Left: a distance-time graph with a straight sloping line and a dashed triangle showing that the gradient is the speed. Right: a speed-time graph with the area under the sloping line shaded, showing that the area is the distance moved.

cards.front: On a speed-time graph, what does the gradient give you?
cards.back:
The **rate of change of speed**, in m/s².

A horizontal line means a steady speed; a sloping line means the speed is changing.

cards.front: On a speed-time graph, what does the area under the line give you?
cards.back:
The **distance moved**, in m.

Split the shape into triangles and rectangles, work out each area and add them.

cards.front: Higher: what does the gradient of a displacement-time graph give you?
cards.back:
The **velocity**, in m/s.

A negative gradient means the object is moving back towards the start.

cards.front: Higher: what do the gradient of, and the area under, a velocity-time graph give you?
cards.back:
Gradient = **acceleration** (m/s²).
Area under the line = **displacement** (m).

cards.front: Trap: a velocity-time graph is a straight line sloping steadily upwards. How do you describe the motion?
cards.back:
**Constant acceleration** - not constant speed.

Constant speed is a horizontal line. Examiners report 'constant speed' given for a sloping section as a common loss of marks.

cards.front: Find the distance travelled from a speed-time graph
cards.back:
1 Divide the area under the line into triangles and rectangles.
2 Triangle area = ½ x base x height; rectangle area = base x height.
3 Read base and height off the axes with their units.
4 Add the areas.
5 Answer in metres.

cards.front: A speed-time graph rises in a straight line from 0 to 8 m/s over 4 s. Distance travelled?
cards.back:
**16 m**

area = ½ x 4 x 8 = 16 m

cards.front: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the object is ____.
cards.back:
**stationary** (at rest)

The distance is not changing, so the gradient - and the speed - is zero.

topics.title: Forces in pairs, friction and resultant force

cards.front: How do forces arise between two objects?
cards.back: Always in **pairs**. If object A pushes or pulls object B, then B pushes or pulls A with a force that is equal in size and opposite in direction.

cards.front: Define friction
cards.back: A force that **always opposes motion** - it acts in the opposite direction to the way an object is moving, or trying to move.

cards.front: Force
cards.back: Newton, symbol **N**.

cards.front: How does this specification want the directions of two forces in a line handled?
cards.back: Give a force acting in one direction a **positive** value and a force in the opposite direction a **negative** value. The resultant is then the sum of the signed forces.

cards.front: Find the resultant of two forces acting along the same line
cards.back:
1 Choose which direction counts as positive.
2 Write each force with its sign.
3 Add them.
4 Give the size in newtons **and** the direction of the answer.

cards.front: A car has a driving force of 30 N forwards and 12 N of friction. Resultant force?
Balanced forces give a resultant force of ____ N, so the motion of the object does not change.
cards.back:
**0**

The object stays still, or keeps moving in a straight line at a constant speed.

topics.title: Newton's first and second laws; F = ma

cards.front: State Newton's first law
cards.back: With **no unbalanced force** acting, an object carries on moving in a straight line at a constant speed (or stays at rest).

cards.front: What does Newton's second law say?
cards.back: A **resultant force** makes an object accelerate, and the acceleration is **proportional to the size of the resultant force**.

cards.front: Equation for Newton's second law
cards.back:
In words: resultant force = mass x acceleration.

In symbols: $F = m \times a$

Units: F in N, m in kg, a in m/s².

Rearranged: $m = \frac{F}{a}$ and $a = \frac{F}{m}$.

cards.front: F = 12 N, a = 3 m/s²: mass?
m = 1500 kg, a = 0.8 m/s²: resultant force?
A 2 kg mass on a rope accelerates upwards at 2 m/s². Find the force in the rope.
cards.back:
1 Weight first: $W = mg = 2 \times 10 = 20$ N down.
2 Resultant needed: $F = ma = 2 \times 2 = 4$ N up.
3 Rope force = weight + resultant = 20 + 4 = **24 N**.

Newton II questions that need the weight before the upward force were poorly done.

cards.front: How can Newton's first and second laws be investigated experimentally?
cards.back:
1 Use an air track (or a simulation) so friction is almost removed.
2 Keep the mass fixed, apply different forces and record the acceleration with a data logger.
3 Plot acceleration against force: a straight line through the origin.
4 Repeat with the same force and different masses.

cards.front: Trap: the mass in a question is given in grams. What must happen before F = ma?
cards.back: Divide by 1000 to get **kilograms**. F = ma only works with the mass in kg; a mass left in grams makes the force 1000 times too big.

topics.title: Mass, weight and free fall

cards.front: Define mass
cards.back:
The **amount of matter** in an object, measured in kilograms (kg).

It is the same wherever the object is taken.
cards.source: CCEA DA Physics Glossary; CER March 2026 P1

cards.front: Define weight
cards.back: The **force** acting on an object due to the **pull of gravity**, measured in newtons (N).

cards.front: Equation for weight
cards.back:
In words: weight = mass x gravitational field strength.

In symbols: $W = m \times g$, with $g = 10$ N/kg on Earth.

Units: W in N, m in kg, g in N/kg.

Rearranged: $m = \frac{W}{g}$.

cards.front: A bag has a mass of 4.5 kg. Weight on Earth?
cards.back:
**45 N**

$W = m \times g = 4.5 \times 10 = 45$ N

cards.front: Two balls of different mass are dropped together where there is no air resistance. Which lands first?
cards.back: **Neither** - they land together. Without air resistance all objects fall at the same rate, whatever their mass.

cards.front: By how much does the speed of an object dropped from rest change each second?
cards.back: It increases by **10 m/s every second** that it falls (on Earth, with no air resistance).

cards.front: Higher: what is the acceleration of free fall?
cards.back:
$g = 10$ **m/s²** for an object falling freely from rest.

The same letter g is 10 N/kg when it is used as gravitational field strength in $W = mg$.

cards.front: Trap: a 70 kg toolbox is taken to the Moon. What changes, mass or weight?
cards.back:
**Weight** changes, because the pull of gravity is weaker there. The mass stays 70 kg because the amount of matter is unchanged.

Mass is in kg; weight is a force in N.

topics.title: Hooke's law and the spring constant

cards.front: State Hooke's law in full
cards.back: The **extension** of a spring is **directly proportional** to the **force applied**, provided the **limit of proportionality** is not exceeded.

cards.front: Trap: is 'provided the elastic limit is not exceeded' accepted in Hooke's law?
cards.back:
**No.** Examiners accept only **limit of proportionality**.

The full statement needs all three ideas: extension, directly proportional to force, and the limit of proportionality.

cards.front: Equation for Hooke's law
cards.back:
In words: force = spring constant x extension.

In symbols: $F = k \times e$

Units: F in N, k in N/m (or N/cm), e in m (or cm).

Rearranged: $k = \frac{F}{e}$ and $e = \frac{F}{k}$.

cards.front: How is the extension of a spring worked out from measurements?
cards.back:
extension = stretched length **-** original (unstretched) length.

The stretched length on its own is not the extension.

cards.front: Force (y-axis) is plotted against extension (x-axis). What does the gradient give, and what happens at the point marked L?
cards.back:
The gradient is numerically equal to the **spring constant k**.

Up to L the line is straight through the origin, so extension is proportional to force. Past L, the limit of proportionality, the line bends and Hooke's law no longer holds.

image.alt: A force against extension graph: a straight line from the origin up to a marked point L, after which the line curves and flattens. A dashed triangle on the straight part is labelled gradient = k.
image.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 250 176' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'><path d='M44 140 L44 16 M44 140 L232 140'/><path d='M44 140 L154 46'/><path d='M154 46 C182 30 206 26 224 24'/><circle cx='154' cy='46' r='3' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'/><path d='M60 126 L104 126 L104 88' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><g font-size='9' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'><text x='4' y='12'>force (N)</text><text x='160' y='158'>extension (cm)</text><text x='60' y='112'>gradient = k</text><text x='160' y='42'>L</text><text x='4' y='172'>L = limit of proportionality</text></g></svg>

cards.front: A force of 6 N stretches a spring by 0.04 m. Spring constant?
A spring has k = 25 N/cm. Force needed for an extension of 3 cm?
cards.back:
**75 N**

$F = k \times e = 25 \times 3 = 75$ N

cards.front: Prescribed Practical P2: how the extension of a spring depends on the force
cards.back:
1 Hang the spring from a clamp and record its original length.
2 Add a known weight; measure the new length with a ruler at eye level.
3 extension = new length - original length.
4 Repeat for several weights.
5 Plot force (y) against extension (x): a straight line through the origin up to the limit of proportionality.

cards.front: Trap: you calculate k = 2.5 and write no unit. What is lost?
cards.back: A mark. The unit must match the extension you used: **N/cm** if the extension was in cm, **N/m** if it was in m. The unit of the answer is often a separate mark.

topics.title: Pressure = force / area

cards.front: Define pressure
cards.back:
The **force exerted on each square metre** of a surface.

Its unit is the pascal (Pa), and 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

cards.front: Equation for pressure
cards.back:
In words: pressure = force divided by area.

In symbols: $P = \frac{F}{A}$

Units: P in Pa (N/m²), F in N, A in m².

Rearranged: $F = P \times A$ and $A = \frac{F}{P}$.

cards.front: Pressure
cards.back: Pascal, symbol **Pa**, and 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

cards.front: A pressure question gives the area in cm². Do you convert to m²?
cards.back:
**No.** This specification sets questions in cm² and mm² and does not expect a conversion to m².

Just keep the unit consistent: an area in cm² gives a pressure in N/cm².

cards.front: A force of 60 N acts on an area of 0.5 m². Pressure?
A pressure of 200 Pa acts over 0.3 m². Force?
cards.back:
**60 N**

$F = P \times A = 200 \times 0.3 = 60$ N

cards.front: Why does a sharp knife cut easily, and why do caterpillar tracks stop a vehicle sinking?
cards.back:
The knife blade has a **small area**, so the same force gives a **large pressure**.

Caterpillar tracks spread the weight over a **large area**, so the pressure on the ground is **small**.

topics.title: Moment of a force and the Principle of Moments

cards.front: Define the moment of a force
cards.back:
The **turning effect** of a force about a pivot:

moment = force x **perpendicular distance from the pivot**.

cards.front: Moment of a force
cards.back:
**Newton metre, N m** (newtons multiplied by metres).

With the distance in centimetres the unit is N cm.

cards.front: Trap: a student writes the unit of a moment as N/m. Why is that wrong?
cards.back:
A moment is force **multiplied** by distance, so the unit is **N m**, never N/m or N/cm.

Examiners call this one of the most poorly answered points in the physics practical paper.
cards.source: CER Summer 2025 U7B Physics; CER March 2026 P1

cards.front: Trap: you have found a moment of 12 N m. What else does the answer need?
cards.back:
Its **direction**: clockwise or anticlockwise.

A moment is a turning effect, so the mark scheme asks for the way it turns as well as its size.

cards.front: State the Principle of Moments
cards.back: When an object is **in equilibrium**, the sum of the **clockwise moments about a point** equals the sum of the **anticlockwise moments about that same point**.

cards.front: Trap: which two phrases do candidates leave out of the Principle of Moments?
cards.back:
**'when the object is in equilibrium'** and **'about a point'** (the pivot).

Without both, the statement does not score full marks.
cards.source: CER Summer 2025 U7B Physics; CER Summer 2023 P1 (H)

cards.front: Equation for the moment of a force
cards.back:
In words: moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot.

In symbols: moment $= F \times d$

Units: N m (F in N, d in m).

Rearranged: $F = \frac{\text{moment}}{d}$ and $d = \frac{\text{moment}}{F}$.

cards.front: On this balanced beam, which force gives the clockwise moment and which the anticlockwise moment?
cards.back:
F2, on the **right** of the pivot, turns the beam **clockwise**.
F1, on the **left**, turns it **anticlockwise**.

In equilibrium: $F_1 \times d_1 = F_2 \times d_2$, with both distances measured from the pivot.

image.alt: A horizontal beam resting on a triangular pivot near its centre, with a downward force F1 at distance d1 to the left of the pivot and a downward force F2 at distance d2 to the right. The left force is labelled anticlockwise moment and the right force clockwise moment.

cards.front: A 25 N force acts at right angles to a spanner, 0.4 m from the pivot. Moment?
cards.back:
**10 N m, clockwise or anticlockwise as drawn**

moment $= F \times d = 25 \times 0.4 = 10$ N m

cards.front: A 4 N weight 30 cm left of the pivot balances an unknown weight 20 cm to the right. The unknown weight?
cards.back:
**6 N**

anticlockwise = clockwise, so $4 \times 30 = W \times 20$, giving $W = \frac{120}{20} = 6$ N

cards.front: Use the Principle of Moments to find an unknown force or distance
cards.back:
1 Mark the pivot and measure every distance from it.
2 List the clockwise moments (force x distance) and the anticlockwise moments.
3 The object is in equilibrium, so set the two sums equal.
4 Leave the unknown as the only letter and solve.
5 Give the unit, and a direction if a force is asked for.

cards.front: Trap: the diagram labels distances from the end of the metre rule, not from the pivot. What now?
cards.back:
Work out each distance **from the pivot** before multiplying.

A moment uses the perpendicular distance from the pivot, so using the printed numbers straight from the diagram loses the marks.

cards.front: Trap: a beam carries two loads and rests on one support. What is the upward force at the support?
cards.back:
The **sum** of the downward forces - the two loads (plus the beam's weight if given).

Candidates lost marks by subtracting the loads instead of adding them.

cards.front: Prescribed Practical P3: verifying the Principle of Moments
cards.back:
1 Balance a metre rule on a pivot at its centre of gravity.
2 Hang a known weight on one side; record its distance from the pivot.
3 Hang a second weight on the other side and slide it until the rule balances.
4 Record both weights and both distances from the pivot.
5 Compare force x distance on each side.

topics.title: Centre of gravity and stability

cards.front: Define the centre of gravity
cards.back: The point on an object where **all of its weight** may be considered **to act**.

cards.front: Trap: 'the centre of gravity is where the gravity of an object is'. What is missing?
cards.back:
Two things examiners insist on: the word **weight** (not 'gravity') and the word **acts**.

The answer must say that all the weight of the object can be taken to act at that point.
cards.source: CER Summer 2025 U7B Physics; CER Summer 2024 P1 (H)

cards.front: Where is the centre of gravity of a disc, a rectangle and a ring?
cards.back:
At the **geometric centre** of each: the centre of the disc, the point where the diagonals of the rectangle cross, and the middle of the hole in a ring.

For the ring it lies outside the material of the object.

cards.front: What makes an object more stable?
cards.back:
A **low centre of gravity** and a **wide base**.

Both mean the object has to be tilted much further before it topples.

cards.front: Trap: 'it is more stable because it has more area'. Why does that score nothing?
cards.back:
Stability is explained by the **height of the centre of gravity** and the **width of the base**, never by 'area' or 'surface area'.

This is one of the most common wrong reasons in the reports.
cards.source: CER Summer 2025 U7B Physics; CER Summer 2024 P1 (H)

cards.front: When does a tilted object topple over?
cards.back:
When the **vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base**.

The weight then has a turning effect about the tipping edge and pulls the object over.

cards.front: When does the weight of an object have a turning effect?
cards.back:
Whenever the **line of action of the weight does not pass through the pivot**.

The weight then acts at a perpendicular distance from the pivot, so it has a moment about it.

cards.front: A double-decker bus is made safer by putting the heavy engine low down, which ____ its centre of gravity.
cards.back:
**lowers**

A lower centre of gravity, together with a wide wheelbase, makes the bus harder to topple.

topics.title: Density and kinetic theory

cards.front: Equation for density
cards.back:
In words: density = mass divided by volume.

In symbols: $D = \frac{m}{V}$

Units: g/cm³ or kg/m³.

Rearranged: $m = D \times V$ and $V = \frac{m}{D}$.

cards.front: Trap: a student writes density = mass x volume. How do you check yourself?
cards.back:
Density is mass **divided by** volume - how much mass is packed into each cm³.

Multiplying is the single most common density error in the reports, and it makes the answer far too large.

cards.front: Density, and the link between its two units
cards.back:
g/cm³ and kg/m³.

**1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³**, so water is 1 g/cm³ or 1000 kg/m³.

cards.front: Measure the density of an irregular solid that sinks in water
cards.back:
1 Find the mass on a balance, in g.
2 Find the volume by **displacement**: lower the solid into a part-filled measuring cylinder and take the rise in level, or catch the overflow from a eureka can.
3 density = mass / volume, in g/cm³.

cards.front: Trap: finding the volume of an irregular stone by measuring it with a ruler. What is wrong?
cards.back:
Length x width x height only works for a **regular** solid.

An irregular solid needs the **displacement method** - a measuring cylinder or a eureka can. Examiners report the displacement method being missed.

cards.front: Use kinetic theory to explain why a gas has a much lower density than a solid
cards.back:
In a solid the particles are **closely packed**, so a lot of mass fits into a small volume.

In a gas the particles are **far apart**, so the same number of particles fills a far bigger volume. Liquids come between the two.

cards.front: A block has a mass of 240 g and a volume of 30 cm³. Density?
cards.back:
**8 g/cm³**

$D = \frac{m}{V} = \frac{240}{30} = 8$ g/cm³

cards.front: A liquid of density 2.5 g/cm³ fills 12 cm³. Mass?
cards.back:
**30 g**

$m = D \times V = 2.5 \times 12 = 30$ g

cards.front: Find the density of a liquid from a mass-volume graph
cards.back:
1 Weigh an empty measuring cylinder.
2 Add a known volume of the liquid and weigh again; mass of liquid = difference.
3 Repeat for several volumes.
4 Plot mass (y) against volume (x): a straight line through the origin.
5 The gradient is the density, in g/cm³.

topics.title: Forms of energy, conservation of energy and efficiency

cards.front: Name the forms of energy listed in this specification
cards.back: Chemical, heat, electrical, sound, light, magnetic, strain, kinetic and gravitational potential.

cards.front: Trap: which of power, weight, pressure, force and heat is a form of energy?
cards.back:
**Heat** only. Power, weight, pressure and force are not forms of energy.

Examiners report all four being offered as energy forms, and heat being missed.

cards.front: State the Principle of Conservation of Energy
cards.back: Energy can be **changed from one form to another**, but the **total amount of energy does not change**.
keyWords: changed from one form to another

cards.front: Energy is measured in what unit, and how big is one of them?
cards.back:
The **joule (J)**.

1 J is roughly the energy needed to lift an apple one metre vertically.

cards.front: Draw an energy transfer diagram for a device
cards.back:
1 Write the input energy form on the left.
2 Draw an arrow into the device.
3 Branch the output arrows: the useful form first, then the wasted forms (usually heat and sound).
4 Label every arrow with a form of energy.
5 The total energy out equals the energy in.

cards.front: Trap: give the energy change in a loudspeaker, and the input energy of a solar panel.
cards.back:
Loudspeaker: **electrical to sound** (plus wasted heat) - candidates often write it backwards.

Solar panel: the input is **light energy** from the Sun, not heat or electrical energy.

cards.front: Why is no device 100% efficient?
cards.back:
Not all of the input energy comes out in the useful form; some is always transferred to less useful forms, usually **heat** and **sound**.

The total energy is still conserved - it has just spread out.

cards.front: Define efficiency
cards.back: The **fraction of the total input energy** that is **transferred usefully** by a device.

cards.front: Equation for efficiency
cards.back:
In words: efficiency = useful output energy divided by total input energy.

Quote it as a **decimal** or multiply by 100 for a **percentage**.

Energies in J; efficiency itself has **no unit** and can never be more than 1 (100%).

cards.front: A lamp takes in 400 J and gives out 120 J of light. Efficiency as a percentage?

topics.title: Renewable and non-renewable energy resources

cards.front: Define a renewable energy resource
cards.back: Energy collected from a resource that is **replaced within a human lifetime**, so it will **never run out**.

cards.front: Define a non-renewable energy resource
cards.back: Energy from a resource that **cannot be replaced within a human lifetime**, so the supply is finite and it will **run out**.

cards.front: Name the renewable energy resources named in this specification
cards.back: Sunlight, wind, hydroelectricity, tidal, waves, **wood** and geothermal heat.

cards.front: Trap: is wood renewable, and is nuclear renewable?
cards.back:
**Wood is renewable** - trees regrow well within a human lifetime.
**Nuclear is non-renewable** - supplies of uranium ore will not last forever.

Both were reversed by candidates in March 2026.

cards.front: Which resources count as non-renewable, and why?
cards.back: The fossil fuels - **oil, natural gas and coal** - because they cannot be replaced in a human lifetime, and **nuclear** fuel, because uranium ore is finite.

cards.front: Give two environmental drawbacks of using renewable resources
cards.back: **Habitat destruction** (for example flooding a valley for hydroelectricity) and **visual pollution** (for example wind turbines on a landscape).

cards.front: Give two environmental effects of using non-renewable resources
cards.back: **Acid rain** and **global warming**, both from the gases released when fossil fuels are burned.

cards.front: Nuclear energy based on fission is ____ because supplies of uranium ore will not last forever.
cards.back: **non-renewable**

topics.title: Work done and power

cards.front: When is work said to be done?
cards.back:
When **energy changes from one form to another**.

The work done is equal to the energy transferred, so both are measured in joules.

cards.front: Equation for work done
cards.back:
In words: work = force x distance moved in the direction of the force.

In symbols: $W = F \times d$

Units: W in J, F in N, d in m.

Rearranged: $F = \frac{W}{d}$ and $d = \frac{W}{F}$.

cards.front: Define power
cards.back: The amount of **energy transferred in one second** - equally, the work done in one second.

cards.front: Trap: why do 'power is energy', 'power is force' and 'power is strength' all score nothing?
cards.back:
Power is a **rate**. The definition must link energy (or work) **to time**: the energy transferred **per second**.

Examiners called the power definition the most challenging part of the whole P1 Higher paper.

cards.front: Power
cards.back:
Watt, symbol **W**.

1 W = 1 joule per second (1 J/s).

cards.front: The two equations for power
cards.back:
$P = \frac{E}{t}$ (power = energy transferred / time taken)
$P = \frac{W}{t}$ (power = work done / time taken)

Units: P in W, E and W in J, t in s.

Rearranged: $E = P \times t$ and $t = \frac{E}{P}$.

cards.front: A box is pulled 2 m along the floor by a force of 250 N. Work done?
cards.back:
**500 J**

$W = F \times d = 250 \times 2 = 500$ J

cards.front: 600 J of work is done in 4 s. Power?
A 50 W motor does 900 J of work. Time taken?
Prescribed Practical P4: measuring your personal power
cards.back:
1 Find your weight in newtons: $W = mg$ with g = 10 N/kg.
2 Measure the vertical height climbed (one stair x the number of stairs), in metres.
3 Time the climb with a stopclock; repeat and take a mean.
4 work done = weight x height.
5 personal power = work done / time, in watts.

cards.front: Trap: a forklift raises a load 120 cm. What must change before W = F x d?
cards.back:
Convert to **metres**: 120 cm = 1.2 m.

Candidates who left the distance in centimetres lost two of the four marks on this exact question.

cards.front: Trap: a question gives the time as 3 minutes. What goes into P = E / t?
cards.back:
**180 s**. Every power and energy equation on this course needs the time in **seconds**.

Minutes left unconverted is one of the most repeated errors in the reports.

topics.title: Kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy

cards.front: Define kinetic energy
cards.back: The energy a body has **due to its motion**.

cards.front: Equation for kinetic energy
cards.back:
In words: kinetic energy = half x mass x speed squared.

In symbols: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

Units: $E_k$ in J, m in kg, v in m/s.

Square the speed **before** halving.

cards.front: Trap: a kinetic energy question gives the mass as 250 g. What goes into the equation?
cards.back:
**0.25 kg** - divide grams by 1000 first.

A mass left in grams was the commonest arithmetic slip in the Higher kinetic energy question.

cards.front: Define gravitational potential energy
cards.back: The energy a body has **due to its height above the Earth's surface**.

cards.front: Equation for gravitational potential energy
cards.back:
In words: gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x vertical height.

In symbols: $E_p = mgh$, with g = 10 N/kg.

Units: $E_p$ in J, m in kg, h in m.

Rearranged: $h = \frac{E_p}{mg}$ and $m = \frac{E_p}{gh}$.

cards.front: Trap: a student writes potential energy = mass x height. What is missing?
cards.back:
**g**, the 10 N/kg. $E_p = m \times g \times h$.

Leaving g out is reported in more than one series, and the height must be the **vertical** height.

cards.front: What happens to the energy of a ball as it falls, if air resistance is ignored?
cards.back:
**Gravitational potential energy lost = kinetic energy gained.**

So $mgh$ at the top becomes $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ at the bottom, and the total energy stays the same.

cards.front: Trap: a ball already has 10 J of kinetic energy at the top and gains 100 J as it falls. Energy at the bottom?
cards.back:
**110 J** - add the energy the object started with.

A large number of candidates ignored or subtracted the initial 10 J. Then obey any instruction about decimal places.

cards.front: m = 0.4 kg, v = 30 m/s. Kinetic energy?
m = 250 g, v = 4 m/s. Kinetic energy?
cards.back:
**2 J**

250 g = 0.25 kg, so $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.25 \times 16 = 2$ J

cards.front: m = 2 kg lifted to h = 15 m. Gravitational potential energy gained?
cards.back:
**300 J**

$E_p = mgh = 2 \times 10 \times 15 = 300$ J

cards.front: A 3 kg mass gains 90 J of potential energy. Height raised?
cards.back:
**3 m**

$h = \frac{E_p}{mg} = \frac{90}{3 \times 10} = 3$ m

cards.front: Find the speed of a dropped object when it lands, using energy
cards.back:
1 $E_p$ at the top $= mgh$ (add any energy it already had).
2 All of it becomes kinetic energy: $E_k = E_p$.
3 Put it into $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ and rearrange: $v^2 = \frac{2E_k}{m}$.
4 Square root for v, in m/s.
5 Mass in kg throughout.

topics.title: Structure of the atom and nucleus; nuclide notation and isotopes

cards.front: Give the relative charge and relative mass of a proton, a neutron and an electron
cards.back:
Proton: charge +1, mass 1.
Neutron: charge 0, mass 1.
Electron: charge -1, mass **1/1840**.

cards.front: Where are the protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom?
cards.back:
Protons and neutrons are packed together in the tiny central **nucleus**; the electrons orbit around it in shells.

Almost all the mass is in the nucleus.

cards.front: Define mass number
cards.back:
The **number of protons and neutrons** in an atom.

Symbol A, written as the upper number in nuclide notation.

cards.front: Define atomic number
cards.back:
The **number of protons** in an atom.

Symbol Z, written as the lower number in nuclide notation.

cards.front: Read a nucleus written in nuclide notation
cards.back:
1 The symbol X is the element.
2 The **upper** number is the mass number A.
3 The **lower** number is the atomic number Z.
4 Protons = Z; electrons = Z in a neutral atom.
5 Neutrons = **A - Z**.

cards.front: Explain what an isotope is
cards.back: Atoms of the **same element** with the **same atomic number** but **different mass numbers** - that is, the same number of protons and a different number of neutrons.

cards.front: An atom has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. Protons, neutrons and electrons?
cards.back:
**11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons**

neutrons = A - Z = 23 - 11 = 12

cards.front: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have Z = 6. How many neutrons has each, and what are they called?
cards.back: 6 neutrons and 8 neutrons. They are **isotopes** of carbon: the same atomic number, different mass numbers.

cards.front: The number of neutrons in a nucleus is the mass number minus the ____ number.
cards.back:
**atomic**

neutrons = A - Z

topics.title: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation; penetration and decay equations

cards.front: What does radioactive mean?
cards.back: An **unstable nucleus** decays to become more stable, **giving out radiation** - alpha, beta or gamma.

cards.front: How do examiners want radioactive decay described in time?
cards.back: It happens **randomly** and **spontaneously**: you cannot say which nucleus will decay next or when, and nothing done to the source starts it off.

cards.front: Define an alpha particle
cards.back: A particle of **2 protons and 2 neutrons** - a **helium nucleus** - emitted from an unstable nucleus in radioactive decay.

cards.front: Define a beta particle
cards.back: A **fast-moving electron** emitted from an unstable nucleus in radioactive decay.

cards.front: Define a gamma ray
cards.back: A **high-energy electromagnetic wave** emitted from an unstable nucleus in radioactive decay.

cards.front: What stops alpha, beta and gamma radiation, and how far does each travel in air?
cards.back:
**Alpha**: a thin sheet of paper, or a few centimetres of air.
**Beta**: a thin sheet of aluminium, or several metres of air.
**Gamma**: passes through both; it is blocked by thick **lead**.

image.alt: A radioactive source on the left emitting three horizontal rays. The alpha ray is stopped at a thin sheet of paper, the beta ray at a thicker sheet of aluminium, and the gamma ray at a very thick block of lead.

cards.front: Higher: balance a nuclear decay equation
cards.back:
1 The **mass numbers** (upper) must add up to the same on both sides.
2 The **atomic numbers** (lower) must add up to the same on both sides.
3 Find any missing number by subtraction.
4 Check the particle: helium-4 for alpha; an electron with 0 above and -1 below for beta.

cards.front: Higher: what does alpha decay do to A and Z?
cards.back:
$^{A}_{Z}X \rightarrow\ ^{A-4}_{Z-2}Y + ^{4}_{2}He$

The mass number falls by **4** and the atomic number falls by **2**, because a helium nucleus leaves.

cards.front: Higher: what does beta decay do to A and Z?
cards.back:
$^{A}_{Z}X \rightarrow\ ^{A}_{Z+1}Y + ^{\ 0}_{-1}e$

The mass number is **unchanged** and the atomic number goes **up by 1**.

cards.front: Higher: what does gamma emission do to A and Z?
cards.back:
$^{A}_{Z}X \rightarrow\ ^{A}_{Z}X + \gamma$

**Neither** the mass number nor the atomic number changes - the nucleus simply loses energy.

cards.front: Trap: in a beta decay equation, which way does the atomic number go and how is the electron written?
cards.back:
The atomic number goes **up by one**, and the beta particle is written with mass number **0** on top and atomic number **-1** below.

Both points were specifically flagged as lost marks.

cards.front: Higher: radium-226 (Z = 88) emits an alpha particle. A and Z of the new nucleus?
Higher: carbon-14 (Z = 6) emits a beta particle. A and Z of the new nucleus?
cards.back:
**A = 14, Z = 7**

The mass number is unchanged; the atomic number rises by one.

topics.title: Background radiation, dangers of radiation and safe handling

cards.front: Define background activity
cards.back: The activity still measured when **all known radioactive sources have been removed** from the area.

cards.front: Correct a measured count rate for background
cards.back:
1 Record the count rate with **no source present** - that is the background.
2 Record the count rate with the source in place.
3 **Subtract** the background from the measured value.
4 Use this corrected count rate in any half-life work.

cards.front: Name the natural sources of background activity
cards.back: **Cosmic rays** from space, **rocks and soil** (some containing radioactive elements such as **radon**), and radioactive materials taken up from the soil and passed along the **food chain**.

cards.front: How does human activity add to background activity?
cards.back: Medical **X-rays**, radioactive **waste** from nuclear power plants, and **fallout** from the testing of nuclear weapons.

cards.front: What can be done about a high radon background in a house?
cards.back: Little can be done about natural background in general, but homes in high-radon areas are **well ventilated** so the gas does not build up indoors.

cards.front: Why is radiation dangerous to living cells?
cards.back: It causes **ionisation** by removing electrons from atoms. In the molecules of living cells this damages the **genetic material**, and the cell may become **cancerous**.

cards.front: Which radiation is most dangerous outside the body, and which inside?
cards.back:
**Outside**: beta and gamma, because they penetrate the skin and reach cells; alpha cannot get through the skin.

**Inside** (breathed in or swallowed): **alpha** is the most dangerous, because it ionises strongly in contact with cells.

cards.front: Handle a radioactive source safely in the laboratory
cards.back:
1 Wear protective clothing.
2 Keep the source at a distance by using **tongs**, never fingers.
3 Point it away from people.
4 Keep the exposure **time as short as possible**.
5 Store it in a **lead-lined container**.

cards.front: A source reads 84 counts/min; with no source the detector reads 20 counts/min. Corrected count rate?

topics.title: Half-life

cards.front: Define half-life
cards.back: The **time taken** for the **count rate** (activity) of a radioactive source **to halve**.

cards.front: Trap: 'half-life is the time taken for a source to halve' scores one mark out of two. Why?
cards.back:
It never says **what** is halving. Name it: the **activity**, the **count rate**, or the **number of undecayed nuclei**.

That is exactly where the second mark was lost in the reports.

cards.front: Read a half-life from a decay graph
cards.back:
1 Subtract the background from the readings if you are told it.
2 Read the starting activity A off the y-axis.
3 Find A/2 on the y-axis and go across to the curve.
4 Drop down to the time axis: that time is the half-life T.
5 Check by repeating from A/2 to A/4 - the same time should come out.

image.alt: An activity against time decay curve falling from A. Dashed lines show that the activity reaches A over 2 after a time T and A over 4 after a time 2T.

cards.front: Do a half-life calculation without a graph
cards.back:
1 Write the starting activity.
2 Halve it, and keep halving, counting how many halvings you do.
3 number of half-lives x half-life = total time.
4 Answer with the unit the question used (hours, days, years).

cards.front: Activity falls from 800 Bq to 100 Bq in 12 hours. Half-life?
cards.back:
**4 hours**

800 to 400 to 200 to 100 is 3 halvings, and 12 / 3 = 4 hours.

cards.front: A source has a half-life of 5 days. What fraction is left undecayed after 15 days?
cards.back:
**one eighth (1/8)**

15 / 5 = 3 half-lives, and 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8.

cards.front: A source reads 800 counts/min and has a half-life of 2 hours. Reading after 6 hours?
cards.back:
**100 counts/min**

6 / 2 = 3 half-lives: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100.

cards.front: Trap: a table gives counts of 250, 150 and 100 with a background of 50. What do you halve?
cards.back:
The **corrected** counts: 200, 100 and 50.

Subtract the background from every reading before you start halving, or the half-life comes out wrong.

cards.front: After two half-lives, ____ of the original undecayed nuclei are left.
cards.back: **a quarter (1/4)**

topics.title: Uses of radioactivity and choosing a half-life

cards.front: What is a radioactive tracer used for?
cards.back: To find out **what is happening inside an object without breaking into it** - the radiation is detected from outside.

cards.front: How is radioactivity used to find the route of an underground pipe or a leak?
cards.back:
A **gamma** emitter is added to the liquid in the pipe, and a detector is moved over the ground above it.

Gamma is used because it can pass out through the soil and the pipe wall.

cards.front: How is radioactivity used to control the thickness of metal sheet?
cards.back:
A **beta** source sits on one side of the rollers and a detector on the other.

If the sheet gets thicker the count falls, and the rollers are adjusted automatically. Beta is used because the sheet must partly absorb it.

cards.front: How are plastic syringes sterilised?
cards.back: With **gamma rays**, which pass through the sealed packaging and kill bacteria inside it.

cards.front: How is the function of an organ monitored?
cards.back: A small amount of a radioactive isotope is **injected into the bloodstream**, and the radiation it emits is detected from outside the body to show how the organ is working.

cards.front: Which radiation is used in a smoke alarm, and why?
cards.back:
**Alpha**. It ionises the air inside the alarm so a small current flows; smoke particles absorb the alpha, the current drops and the alarm sounds.

Its short range also means it does not escape from the alarm.

cards.front: How is the half-life of a source chosen for a job?
cards.back: It must be **long enough for the application to work**, but **short enough to do minimal harm** to people or the environment afterwards.

cards.front: Trap: why not use a long half-life alpha source as a medical tracer?
cards.back:
Alpha would be absorbed inside the body instead of reaching the detector, and it ionises strongly, so it damages cells.

A long half-life would also keep the patient radioactive for far longer than the scan needs. Use a **gamma** emitter with a **short** half-life.

topics.title: Nuclear fission and the nuclear-power debate

cards.front: Define nuclear fission
cards.back: A **heavy nucleus**, such as uranium, **absorbs a neutron** and **splits into two lighter nuclei**, giving out **two or three neutrons and energy**.

cards.front: What is a chain reaction?
cards.back:
The neutrons released by one fission go on to be absorbed by other uranium nuclei, causing **further fissions**, which release more neutrons again.

The reaction keeps itself going and the energy released is used to generate electricity.

cards.front: Trap: how do you keep fission and fusion apart in a written answer?
cards.back:
**Fission splits** one heavy nucleus into two lighter ones. **Fusion joins** two light nuclei into one heavier one.

And in both, say **nuclei**, never 'atoms' - that word alone loses marks.

cards.front: Are fission equations needed on this specification?
cards.back:
**No.** For Double Award Science you describe fission in words only; balanced fission equations are not required.

(Alpha, beta and gamma decay equations are required at Higher Tier.)

cards.front: Give one social argument for and one against nuclear power stations
cards.back:
**For**: they create employment for many people.

**Against**: many people are worried about living near a power plant or near the facilities that store the radioactive waste.

cards.front: Which incidents does this specification expect you to be able to refer to?
cards.back: The accidents at nuclear power plants in **Ukraine** and **Japan**, which caused huge economic, health and environmental damage around the plants.

cards.front: Trap: 'nuclear power produces no greenhouse gases at all'. What is the fuller answer?
cards.back: Fission itself releases **no carbon dioxide**, but the **mining, transport and purification of uranium ore** release significant amounts of greenhouse gases.

cards.front: For fission to occur, the uranium nucleus must first absorb a ____.
cards.back:
**neutron**

It then splits into two smaller nuclei and releases energy and several more neutrons.

topics.title: Nuclear fusion

cards.front: Define nuclear fusion
cards.back: **Two light nuclei**, such as hydrogen, are **joined together** to produce a **heavier, more stable nucleus** (helium), **giving out energy**.

cards.front: Trap: in the six-mark fusion question, what do candidates most often describe by mistake?
cards.back:
**Fission** - splitting a heavy nucleus. Fusion is the opposite: light nuclei **joining**.

Very few scored more than two marks on this question, largely because of that confusion.

cards.front: Trap: 'two hydrogen atoms join together to make helium'. What single word costs marks?
cards.back:
**Atoms**. It is the **nuclei** that join in fusion, not whole atoms.

Examiners list this in both the Foundation and Higher fusion reports.

cards.front: Trap: what is the main by-product of fusion?
cards.back:
**Helium**. Energy is **released** by the reaction - it is not the by-product.

'Energy' was the usual wrong answer to this exact question in two series.

cards.front: Where does fusion happen naturally?
cards.back: In **stars**, including our Sun - fusion is the source of a star's energy.

cards.front: What is the fuel for fusion, and why is the supply described as nearly inexhaustible?
cards.back: **Deuterium and tritium**, the isotopes of hydrogen. They are widely available as constituents of **seawater**, so the supply is nearly inexhaustible.

cards.front: Why is the by-product of fusion an environmental advantage?
cards.back: Helium is **inert and non-toxic**, and fusion emits **no carbon dioxide or other greenhouse gases**.

cards.front: How much energy does controlled fusion release per kilogram compared with burning coal, oil or gas?
cards.back: **Four million times more** energy per kilogram than a chemical reaction such as burning a fossil fuel.

cards.front: How much energy does controlled fusion release per kilogram compared with fission?
cards.back: **Four times as much** energy per kilogram as a nuclear fission reaction.

cards.front: Why is fusion not yet generating electricity commercially?
cards.back:
**Very high temperatures** are needed before nuclei will fuse, so reactors and the systems that contain the reaction are **expensive to build**.

It may be another **50 years** before fusion supplies electricity on a commercial scale.

cards.front: Plan a six-mark answer describing nuclear fusion
cards.back:
1 Two **light nuclei** (deuterium and tritium, isotopes of hydrogen).
2 **Join** to form a heavier nucleus.
3 That nucleus is **helium** - the main by-product.
4 **Energy is released**.
5 Very **high temperature** is needed.
6 It happens naturally in the **Sun and stars**.

cards.front: In fusion, two light ____ join to form one heavier one and energy is released.
cards.back: **nuclei**
